summary: This document describes and discusses the textual encodings of PKIX, PKCS, and CMS structures. These encodings, with their BEGIN and END lines, are well known and widely implemented, and this document records how they work.

plainLanguage.summary: Certificates and keys are normally binary data, which does not fit well in email or a text file. This document describes the text form that most tools already use, so that all of them agree on it.

subtitle: The BEGIN/END base64 text format for certificates, keys and requests, written down so every tool agrees.

tldr.problem: Certificates, keys and similar structures are binary, which does not travel well in email or text documents, and many libraries had their own slightly different text format that was similar to but not identical with PEM.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a textual encoding: five hyphens, the word BEGIN and a label, base64 data wrapped at 64 characters, and a matching END line, with one fixed label for each kind of structure.
tldr.outcome: It records the de facto rules and adds recommendations, so that future implementations interoperate with the tools already in use.

today: RFC 7468 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Textual Encoding
sections.content:
Several security-related standards used on the Internet define ASN.1 data formats that are normally encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) or the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER), which are binary, octet-oriented encodings. RFC 7468 is about the textual encodings of certificates, certificate revocation lists and subject public key info from the X.509 profile (RFC 5280), PKCS #10 certification requests (RFC 2986), PKCS #7 cryptographic messages (RFC 2315), Cryptographic Message Syntax (RFC 5652), PKCS #8 private key information (RFC 5208, renamed to One Asymmetric Key in RFC 5958), and attribute certificates (RFC 5755).

A binary format cannot be interchanged in textual transports such as email or text documents. A text-based encoding is also easy to modify with common text editors, for example to concatenate several certificates into a certificate chain with copy-and-paste operations.

The tradition goes back to Privacy-Enhanced Mail (RFC 1421), and the format is still often called PEM encoding, with variations such as OpenPGP ASCII armor (RFC 4880) and the OpenSSH key file format (RFC 4716). For reasons that basically boil down to non-coordination or inattention, many PKIX, PKCS, and CMS libraries implement a text-based encoding that is similar to but not identical with PEM encoding. This document specifies the textual encoding format, articulates the de facto rules that most implementations operate by, and provides recommendations that will promote interoperability. It also provides common nomenclature for the syntax elements, reflecting the evolution of this de facto standard format.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates and keys are normally binary data, which does not fit well in email or a text file. This document describes the text form that most tools already use, so that all of them agree on it.

sections.title: The General Format
sections.content:
Textual encoding begins with a line made of '-----BEGIN ', a label, and '-----', and ends with a line made of '-----END ', a label, and '-----'. Between these encapsulation boundaries is base64-encoded data as defined in Section 4 of RFC 4648. Data before the encapsulation boundaries is permitted, and parsers MUST NOT malfunction when processing it. Parsers SHOULD ignore whitespace and other non-base64 characters and MUST handle different newline conventions.

The type of data encoded is labeled by the type label in the BEGIN line, for example '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----' to indicate a PKIX certificate. Generators MUST put the same label on the END line as on the corresponding BEGIN line. Labels are formally case-sensitive, uppercase, and made of zero or more characters; they do not contain consecutive spaces or hyphen-minuses, nor a space or hyphen-minus at either end. Parsers MAY disregard the label in the END line instead of signalling an error, because some extant implementations require the labels to match and others do not.

There is exactly one space character separating 'BEGIN' or 'END' from the label, and exactly five hyphen-minus characters on both ends of the encapsulation boundaries, no more and no less. The label type implies that the encoded data follows the specified syntax, and parsers MUST handle non-conforming data gracefully. Unlike legacy PEM encoding, OpenPGP ASCII armor, and the OpenSSH key file format, textual encoding does not define or permit headers to be encoded alongside the data.

Generators MUST wrap the base64-encoded lines so that each line consists of exactly 64 characters, except for the final line, which encodes the remainder of the data within the 64-character line boundary, and they MUST NOT emit extraneous whitespace. Parsers MAY handle other line sizes. Files MAY contain multiple textual encoding instances, which is how a file holds several certificates; whether the instances are ordered or unordered depends on the context.
sections.plainLanguage: The shape is fixed. A start line with the word BEGIN and a label, base64 data in lines of 64 characters, and an end line with the word END and the same label. The number of hyphens and spaces is exact, and the document tells parsers how much sloppiness to tolerate.

sections.title: Three Grammars for the Same Format
sections.content:
The document gives three grammars for the same format. The standard ABNF in Figure 1 allows blank space and a missing end-of-line before the base64 body, and treats the base64 padding at the end of the data in a tolerant way. The lax grammar in Figure 2 accepts any mixture of whitespace outside the encapsulation boundaries, which is what the most permissive parser implementations do. The strict grammar in Figure 3 requires an end-of-line after the BEGIN line and after the END line, and requires the base64 body to be exactly 64 characters per line, with a final line of up to 64 characters.

New implementations SHOULD emit the strict format, and the choice of parsing strategy depends on the context of use. The document warns that such lax parsing may run the risk of accepting text that was not intended to be accepted in the first place, for example because the text was a snippet or a sample.

The whitespace rules are spelled out because extant parsers diverge considerably on them. In this document, whitespace means HT (0x09), VT (0x0B), FF (0x0C), SP (0x20), CR (0x0D), and LF (0x0A), while blank means HT and SP, and lines are divided with CRLF, CR, or LF. Most extant parsers ignore blanks at the ends of lines; blanks at the beginnings of lines or in the middle of the base64-encoded data are far less compatible. The ABNF is specific to US-ASCII, and an implementer ought to use the spirit rather than the letter of the rules in environments that are not strictly limited to US-ASCII, since these encodings are also used on archival storage media such as paper or engravings.
sections.plainLanguage: Three grammars describe the same thing. The strict one is tidy and is what new software should write. The lax one accepts almost anything between the markers. The document sets out how much stray whitespace to tolerate, because existing tools differ.

sections.title: Labels and the Structures They Carry
sections.content:
A convenience guide in Figure 4 lists, for each label, the ASN.1 type it carries and the document that defines it. Certificates, certificate revocation lists and public keys use the types from RFC 5280; certification requests use the type from RFC 2986; the PKCS7 label carries a PKCS #7 ContentInfo (RFC 2315); the CMS label carries a CMS ContentInfo (RFC 5652); the PRIVATE KEY label carries a PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo (RFC 5208) or a OneAsymmetricKey (RFC 5958), which are semantically identical and can be distinguished by version number; ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY carries an EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo; ATTRIBUTE CERTIFICATE carries the type from RFC 5755; and PUBLIC KEY carries a SubjectPublicKeyInfo.

The encoded data MUST be a BER encoding, with DER strongly preferred, except for the PKCS7 and CMS labels, which carry a BER-encoded ContentInfo.

Appendix B explains why DER is preferred. DER is a restricted profile of BER, so all DER encodings of data values are BER encodings, but just one of the possible BER encodings is the DER encoding for a data value. Canonical encoding matters when performing cryptographic operations, and it has certain efficiency advantages for parsers. There are three principal reasons: a digital signature is computed over the DER encoding of the semantic content, so providing anything other than the DER encoding is senseless; cryptographic hashes are in practice computed over the DER encoding for identification; and DER always encodes data values in definite-length form, so a parser can anticipate memory or resource usage up front.
sections.plainLanguage: Each label means one specific ASN.1 structure, and the guide in the document lists them all. The data inside is normally DER, the stricter form of BER, because signatures and hashes are computed over the DER bytes.

sections.title: Label Choices and Legacy Variants
sections.content:
Several labels have historical variants, and the document settles which one to use.

Certificates use the 'CERTIFICATE' label. The labels 'X509 CERTIFICATE' and 'X.509 CERTIFICATE' have also been used, so generators MUST NOT generate them and parsers SHOULD NOT treat them as equivalent to 'CERTIFICATE', though a valid exception may be for backwards compatibility, potentially together with a warning. Certificate revocation lists use 'X509 CRL'; the shorter 'CRL' label has rarely been used and is not common today, so generators MUST generate 'X509 CRL' labels and MUST NOT generate 'CRL' labels, and parsers SHOULD NOT treat 'CRL' as equivalent to 'X509 CRL'.

Certification requests use 'CERTIFICATE REQUEST'. The label 'NEW CERTIFICATE REQUEST' is also in wide use; generators MUST generate 'CERTIFICATE REQUEST' labels, and parsers MAY treat 'NEW CERTIFICATE REQUEST' as equivalent to 'CERTIFICATE REQUEST'. PKCS #7 messages use 'PKCS7'. The label 'CERTIFICATE CHAIN' has been in use to denote a degenerate PKCS #7 structure that contains only a list of certificates, but several modern tools do not support it, so generators MUST NOT generate it and parsers SHOULD NOT treat it as equivalent to 'PKCS7'. PKCS #7 has long been superseded by CMS, so implementations SHOULD NOT generate PKCS #7 when CMS is an alternative, and SHOULD generate CMS when it is an alternative, which promotes interoperability and forwards-compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Several labels have older spellings that tools still meet. The document names one label per structure and says which old ones a parser may accept.

sections.title: File Extensions and Explanatory Text
sections.content:
Many tools are known to emit explanatory text before the BEGIN line and after the END line for PKIX certificates, more than for any other type of structure. If such text is emitted, it SHOULD be related to the certificate, for example by providing a textual representation of key data elements in the certificate.

Although textual encodings of PKIX structures can occur anywhere, many tools are known to offer an option to output this encoding when serializing PKIX structures. To promote interoperability and to separate DER encodings from textual encodings, the extension '.crt' SHOULD be used for the textual encoding of a certificate. Implementations should be aware that in spite of this recommendation, many tools still default to encoding certificates in this textual encoding with the extension '.cer'. This does not disturb the official application/pkix-cert registration in RFC 2585, which states that each '.cer' file contains exactly one certificate encoded in DER format; it merely articulates a widespread, de facto alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: Tools often print a few lines of details about a certificate before the text block, which is allowed if the text is about that certificate. The document also recommends the .crt extension for text files, while many tools still write .cer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Data in this format often originates from untrusted sources, so parsers must be prepared to handle unexpected data without causing security vulnerabilities.

Implementers whose implementations rely on canonical representation, or on the ability to fingerprint a particular data object, need to understand that this document does not define canonical encodings. The first ambiguity is introduced by permitting the text-encoded representation instead of the binary BER or DER encodings, but further ambiguities arise when multiple labels are treated as similar. Variations of whitespace and non-base64 alphabetic characters can create further ambiguities. Data encoding ambiguities also create opportunities for side channels. If canonical encodings are desired, the encoded structure must be decoded and processed into a canonical form, namely DER encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Text that arrives from outside can be malformed, so a parser has to survive it. The document also warns that the text form is not a canonical form, so anything that needs one exact representation has to decode the structure to DER first.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE SHAPE OF A TEXTUAL ENCODING, NOT FROM THE RFC

data.title: Textual encoding
data.code:
-----BEGIN <label>-----
<base64 data, 64 characters per line>
<base64 data, last line shorter>
-----END <label>-----

items.title: Strict
items.text: Requires an end-of-line after the BEGIN line and after the END line, and exactly 64 characters per base64 line. New implementations SHOULD emit this.

items.title: Standard
items.text: Allows blank space before the base64 body and tolerates the base64 padding at the end of the data.

items.title: Lax
items.text: Accepts any mixture of whitespace outside the encapsulation boundaries, which is what the most permissive parsers do.
